title: Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness
author: VirtueVigil Editorial Team

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: NOT A WOKE TRAP. The woke elements in Multiverse of Madness are present from the introduction of America Chavez in the first act. Chavez wears a pride pin on her jacket, mentions her two moms, and the character is openly LGBTQ+ from her first appearance. The Illuminati sequence features gender-swapped and race-swapped legacy characters. Nothing is hidden or delayed. The film is upfront about its progressive elements from the opening.

director.name: Sam Raimi
director.ideology: MODERATE. Raimi is an old-school genre filmmaker without a strong public ideological profile. His Spider-Man trilogy (2002-2007) celebrated traditional heroism, responsibility, and sacrifice. He was brought in as a replacement for Scott Derrickson and brought a horror sensibility rather than a political one.
director.profile: Sam Raimi is the legendary horror and superhero director behind the Evil Dead franchise, the original Spider-Man trilogy, and Drag Me to Hell. He pioneered low-budget horror in the 1980s and became one of Hollywood's most commercially successful directors with Spider-Man (2002). After a decade away from directing, he returned to the superhero genre with Multiverse of Madness. His directorial fingerprints are all over the film's horror sequences, jump scares, and creative camera work.

writer.name: Michael Waldron
writer.profile: Michael Waldron was the head writer of the Loki Disney+ series (2021), which introduced the concept of variants and the multiverse to the MCU. He also wrote for Rick and Morty. Waldron replaced previous writer Jade Halley Bartlett. His script makes Wanda the villain, continuing her arc from WandaVision, and introduces America Chavez from the comics.

composer.name: Danny Elfman
composer.profile: Danny Elfman is one of film's most iconic composers, known for his collaborations with Tim Burton (Batman, Edward Scissorhands, The Nightmare Before Christmas) and Sam Raimi (the Spider-Man trilogy). His Multiverse of Madness score revisits his Raimi collaboration with a darker, horror-inflected approach. The musical note battle sequence is one of the film's most inventive set pieces.

top_performers.name: Elizabeth Olsen
top_performers.note: Olsen is extraordinary as a villain. Her Wanda is terrifying not because she's powerful but because she's sympathetic. You understand why she's doing this even as she murders her way through the multiverse. The sequence where she walks through Kamar-Taj, effortlessly killing sorcerers, is one of the most chilling villain entrances in MCU history. Her final act of self-destruction is genuinely tragic.

top_performers.name: Benedict Cumberbatch
top_performers.note: Cumberbatch plays multiple variants of Strange, each with different energy. Defender Strange, Sinister Strange, and our Strange all feel like distinct characters. His willingness to trust America Chavez when every other Strange tried to sacrifice her defines the film's moral thesis.

bottom_performers.name: Xochitl Gomez
bottom_performers.note: Gomez struggles with the weight of the role. America Chavez is meant to be the film's emotional core but she spends most of the runtime as a passive MacGuffin being chased and rescued. Her power activation in the climax feels unearned because the script gives her almost nothing to do before that moment. This is a writing problem more than a performance problem, but Gomez also lacks the screen presence to fill the gaps.

fidelity_casting.summary: America Chavez is adapted from the comics where she is a Latina LGBTQ+ character with two mothers. That aspect is faithful. However, the Illuminati sequence features significant departures: Captain Marvel is Maria Rambeau (Lashana Lynch) instead of Carol Danvers, a Black woman replacing a white woman. Captain Carter (Hayley Atwell) replaces Steve Rogers as Captain America. Reed Richards is played by John Krasinski (fan casting, actually accurate to the character). Charles Xavier is played by Patrick Stewart in his iconic X-Men role (faithful). The Illuminati gender and race swaps are presented as multiverse variants, which provides in-universe justification. Black Bolt is played by Anson Mount, consistent with the Inhumans series.

celebrity_mentions.name: Sam Raimi
celebrity_mentions.context: Raimi returned to superhero filmmaking 15 years after Spider-Man 3. His horror expertise gives the film a distinctly darker tone than typical MCU entries. His visual style, including Dutch angles and jump scares, is immediately recognizable.

celebrity_mentions.name: Elizabeth Olsen
celebrity_mentions.context: Olsen's turn from protagonist in WandaVision to full villain here was controversial. Some fans felt the Darkhold corruption was too abrupt and undid Wanda's character development.

celebrity_mentions.name: Patrick Stewart
celebrity_mentions.context: Stewart's appearance marked the first crossover between the Fox X-Men universe and the MCU. His death at Wanda's hands was shocking and controversial.

content_warnings: Horror-level violence: a character's mouth is sealed shut and his head is blown apart from internal pressure
A character is cut in half by a shield (shown from distance)
A character has her neck snapped on screen
A character is shredded by a magical whip
Zombified corpse of Doctor Strange is reanimated and fights using souls of the damned
Wanda emerges from a gong covered in blood in a genuinely horrifying horror sequence
Jump scares throughout, deliberately constructed by horror filmmaker Sam Raimi
Extended chase sequences with a demonic entity pursuing a teenager
A character possesses her alternate universe counterpart, essentially body-snatching
Children scream in terror at their mother who has been possessed
America Chavez references having 'two moms' and wears a pride pin on her jacket
Occult and witchcraft elements central to the plot: the Darkhold, dreamwalking, possession
Multiple characters die violently, including beloved legacy heroes
Themes of grief, obsession, and a mother driven to murder by loss of her children
parental_guidance.recommendation: This is the most violent and horror-inflected MCU film to date. Sam Raimi's horror background results in genuine scares that push PG-13 to its limits. The deaths of the Illuminati members are shockingly graphic for a Marvel film. Black Bolt's death in particular is nightmare fuel. The occult elements (Darkhold, witchcraft, possession, dreamwalking) are central rather than peripheral. The LGBTQ+ content is limited to Chavez's pride pin and her two mothers, which are mentioned briefly. Parents should be aware that this film is significantly scarier and more violent than typical MCU fare. Not recommended for children under 13.

summary.overall:
Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness is the MCU's most interesting mess. Sam Raimi brings genuine horror filmmaking to a franchise that desperately needed it, Elizabeth Olsen delivers a villain performance for the ages, and the multiverse concept finally gets the unhinged treatment it deserves. It is also a film that introduces a teenage character wearing a pride pin, features an Earth where Captain America is a woman and Captain Marvel is Black, and treats witchcraft as a legitimate power system. The culture war discourse writes itself.

The plot picks up after WandaVision and Spider-Man: No Way Home. Doctor Strange encounters America Chavez, a teenager who can punch star-shaped portals between universes. A demon is hunting her for this power. Strange discovers that Wanda Maximoff, corrupted by the Darkhold, is the one sending the demons. Wanda wants Chavez's power so she can travel to a universe where her sons Billy and Tommy are real and be their mother.

What follows is a multiverse chase that takes Strange and Chavez to Earth-838, where they meet the Illuminati: a council including Captain Carter (Peggy Carter as Captain America), Maria Rambeau as Captain Marvel, Reed Richards, Black Bolt, Professor X, and Mordo. Wanda dreamwalks into her Earth-838 counterpart and systematically murders the entire Illuminati in a sequence that is both thrilling and genuinely disturbing. Black Bolt's death, where Wanda removes his mouth and his own sonic scream implodes his skull, is one of the most horrific images in superhero cinema.

The traditional elements are strongest in the thematic core. Strange's arc is about learning that heroism means trusting others rather than controlling outcomes. Every other Strange variant tried to sacrifice Chavez or seize power. Our Strange is the one who chooses faith in another person. Wanda's story is a cautionary tale about grief consuming you, about a mother whose love for her children twisted into something monstrous. Her final act, destroying the Darkhold across all universes and sacrificing herself, is genuine redemption through self-destruction. These are powerful, classically structured moral arcs.

The woke elements are real but woven into the fabric rather than delivered as lectures. America Chavez is openly LGBTQ+ with two moms, wearing a pride pin throughout the film. This is faithful to the comic character, who has always been LGBTQ+. The film was banned or censored in Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and several other countries because of these elements. The Earth-838 Illuminati features Captain Carter replacing Captain America (woman replacing man) and Maria Rambeau as Captain Marvel (Black woman in the role held by a white woman in the main MCU). These are technically multiverse variants, which provides narrative justification, but the casting choices are clearly intentional representation.

Wanda as villain is a double-edged sword. On one hand, Elizabeth Olsen is magnificent and the story demands a powerful antagonist. On the other hand, taking the MCU's most prominent female character with her own Disney+ show and turning her into a mass-murdering psychopath is a choice. The Darkhold corruption explains it narratively, but it also means the MCU's biggest female hero arc ends with her buried under a mountain.

Raimi's direction elevates everything. The horror sequences are genuinely frightening. The musical note battle between Strange variants is wildly creative. The zombie Strange sequence, where our Strange reanimates his dead variant using the souls of the damned, is the kind of gonzo genre filmmaking the MCU rarely allows. Danny Elfman's score is excellent.

RT Critics: 74%. RT Audience: 86%. Metacritic: 60. IMDB: 6.9. Box office: $955.8M worldwide on $200M budget (net).
summary.verdict_explanation: WOKE LEAN. Margin of -3, falling in the -9 to -3 range. LGBTQ+ representation through America Chavez, gender/race-swapped Illuminati members, witchcraft as power system, and female hero turned villain produce a wokeScore of 13.60. Strange's trust arc, Wanda's redemption through sacrifice, consequences of dark power, and male hero remaining central produce a tradScore of 10.22. The margin is narrow. Both traditional and progressive elements are meaningful to the story.
summary.woke_trap_assessment: NOT A WOKE TRAP. The progressive elements are visible from the first act. Chavez's pride pin is on screen from her introduction. The marketing featured Elizabeth Olsen prominently, and anyone following WandaVision knew the Darkhold storyline. There is no late-film surprise or ideological pivot. This is a film with identifiable woke elements that are present throughout.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults will find more to appreciate here than expected. Sam Raimi is an old-school filmmaker who prioritizes craft over messaging. The horror elements give the film genuine teeth. Strange's arc is about personal responsibility and trusting others rather than seeking control. Wanda's story is a cautionary tale about what happens when grief overrides morality. The LGBTQ+ elements are present but brief: Chavez mentions her two moms and wears a pride pin, and that's essentially it. The Illuminati gender/race swaps are justified as multiverse variants. The witchcraft and occult elements may concern Christian viewers more than the progressive messaging. This is a flawed but ambitious film that rewards engagement.

tropeAudit.name: Heroism Through Trust (Strange's Arc)
tropeAudit.analysis: The film's thesis is that every other Doctor Strange variant failed because they tried to control outcomes alone. Our Strange succeeds because he trusts America Chavez with her own power rather than sacrificing her or seizing it. This is a classically heroic moral: strength through faith in others rather than self-reliance to the point of arrogance. Severity 3, Authenticity High (0.7), Centrality High (1.8). Score: 3 x 0.7 x 1.8 = 3.78.

tropeAudit.name: Redemption Through Sacrifice (Wanda)
tropeAudit.analysis: Wanda spends the film as a murderous villain driven by maternal grief. When she sees her children in Earth-838 recoil from her in terror, she realizes what she has become. She destroys Mount Wundagore and the Darkhold across all universes, apparently killing herself. This is redemption through self-destruction, a deeply traditional narrative structure. The villain recognizes their evil and pays the ultimate price. Severity 3, Authenticity High (0.7), Centrality High (1.8). Score: 3 x 0.7 x 1.8 = 3.78.

tropeAudit.name: Consequences of Dark Power
tropeAudit.analysis: The Darkhold corrupts everyone who uses it. Strange's Earth-838 variant used it and had to be killed by his own allies. Wanda was corrupted by it. The film is clear that forbidden knowledge and dark power exact a terrible price. This is a traditional moral framework: power gained through dark means destroys you. Severity 2, Authenticity High (0.7), Centrality Moderate (1.0). Score: 2 x 0.7 x 1.0 = 1.40.

tropeAudit.name: Male Hero Remains Central
tropeAudit.analysis: Despite the prominence of Wanda and Chavez, Doctor Strange remains the protagonist and moral center of his own film. He makes the key decisions, drives the plot, and his character growth is the emotional through-line. He is not sidelined, emasculated, or upstaged by the female characters. Severity 2, Authenticity High (0.7 - it's his franchise), Centrality Low (0.5 - this is structural, not thematic). Score: 2 x 0.7 x 0.5 = 0.70.

tropeAudit.name: Maternal Love as Motivation
tropeAudit.analysis: Wanda's motivation is entirely maternal. She wants her children. This is not framed as wrong in itself; it is framed as tragic. The desire for motherhood is treated with genuine sympathy even as the methods are condemned. This is a subtle but real affirmation of maternal instinct as a powerful, legitimate drive. Severity 1 (the affirmation is present but the character is a villain), Authenticity High (0.7 - organic to WandaVision), Centrality Moderate (0.8 effective). Score: 1 x 0.7 x 0.8 = 0.56.

tropeAudit.name: LGBTQ+ Representation (America Chavez)
tropeAudit.analysis: America Chavez wears a pride pin on her denim jacket throughout the film. She mentions having two moms who were accidentally sent to another universe when her powers first manifested. The character is openly LGBTQ+ in the comics and the adaptation is faithful. The pride pin is visible but not commented on. The two moms are mentioned naturally in backstory rather than delivered as a speech. High authenticity significantly reduces the score. Severity 3, Authenticity High (0.7 - faithful to source material), Centrality Moderate (1.0). Score: 3 x 0.7 x 1.0 = 2.10.

tropeAudit.name: Gender-Swapped Legacy Heroes (Illuminati)
tropeAudit.analysis: Captain Carter replaces Captain America. Maria Rambeau replaces Carol Danvers as Captain Marvel. These are multiverse variants, which provides in-universe justification, but the casting choices are clearly intentional diversity representation. Captain Carter exists in the comics (What If). Maria Rambeau as Captain Marvel is a new creation. The Illuminati sequence is a major set piece but they are all killed quickly, which somewhat undermines the representation. Severity 3, Authenticity Moderate (1.0 - mixed source fidelity), Centrality Moderate (1.0). Score: 3 x 1.0 x 1.0 = 3.00.

tropeAudit.name: Witchcraft / Occult as Legitimate Power System
tropeAudit.analysis: Witchcraft, the Darkhold, dreamwalking, and chaos magic are central to the plot. While the film does show consequences for dark magic use, the power system itself is treated as legitimate and morally neutral. Strange himself uses the Darkhold and reanimates a corpse. For conservative Christian viewers, the normalization of witchcraft as a tool rather than an inherent evil is concerning. However, this is deeply authentic to the Doctor Strange comics, which have always been about sorcery. Severity 2, Authenticity High (0.7 - core to source material), Centrality High (1.8). Score: 2 x 0.7 x 1.8 = 2.52.

tropeAudit.name: Female Hero Turned Villain
tropeAudit.analysis: Wanda Maximoff, the MCU's most prominent female Avenger with her own solo series, is turned into a mass-murdering villain. While Elizabeth Olsen is spectacular in the role, the pattern of taking powerful female characters and making them unhinged villains can be read as anti-feminist. Alternatively, some see it as powerful storytelling that treats a female character with the same moral complexity as male characters. The discourse is genuinely split. This is categorized as woke because the surrounding media framing emphasized the problematic treatment of a female character. Severity 2, Authenticity Moderate (1.0 - debatable direction), Centrality High (1.8). Score: 2 x 1.0 x 1.8 = 3.60.

tropeAudit.name: Diverse Supporting Cast
tropeAudit.analysis: Wong (Benedict Wong, Chinese-British) is the Sorcerer Supreme. Mordo (Chiwetel Ejiofor, Black British-Nigerian) leads the Earth-838 variant. America Chavez (Xochitl Gomez, Mexican-American) is the key supporting character. The diversity is organic to the story's global scope and multiverse concept. Severity 2, Authenticity High (0.7 - organic to setting), Centrality Low (0.5). Score: 2 x 0.7 x 0.5 = 0.70.

tropeAudit.name: Teen Girl as Key to Everything
tropeAudit.analysis: America Chavez, a teenage Latina girl, holds the most powerful ability in the multiverse. Every faction wants her power. She's the MacGuffin for most of the film but gets an empowerment moment at the climax when she takes control of her abilities. The 'special teen girl' trope is common in progressive storytelling, but Chavez is established in the comics. The execution is somewhat generic. Severity 2, Authenticity High (0.7 - comic character), Centrality Moderate (1.2 effective). Score: 2 x 0.7 x 1.2 = 1.68.
